##  {background-iframe="assets/bokeh.html"}

<!--
BACKGROUND ANIMATION: the floating blobs are live CSS animation, not
video. assets/bokeh.html is a self-contained page: ~50 lines of CSS
keyframes drive 18 absolutely-positioned blurred radial-gradient circles
(each drifts on a 14-23s transform loop and pulses opacity/scale on a
6-9.5s loop; negative animation-delays de-sync them, so the ensemble
never visibly repeats; mix-blend-mode screen merges overlaps into glow).
The documented background-iframe attribute renders that page as this
slide's full-bleed background layer, behind the content and with pointer
events off, so the deck's own markdown stays plain.

Trade-offs of this route: screenshot/PDF export freezes it at a frame
(verified working); embed-resources does NOT inline iframes, so a
single-file delivery render needs the assets folder alongside, or swap
this attribute for background-image="assets/bokeh.png" (the static
version of the same art). Reserve background-video for content footage;
decorative motion is better served by CSS like this, which is
resolution-independent, seamless and a few KB.
-->

<!--
A designed keynote built from documented Quarto features only:
documented options, Sass variables, pandoc divs/spans with typography-only
and simple-box classes, one executable figure, pre-rendered background art
attached via the documented background-image attribute. No raw HTML, no
positioning CSS. The empty ## headings give full control of content order
on designed slides while staying inside markdown.
-->

[CHAPTER ONE]{.section-label}
[The question every student asks]{.slide-title}

::: {.spread}

[“Why am I learning this?”]{.big-quote}

::: {.body-text .narrow-text}
I am going to answer that today, with a story. It starts with a
[straight line]{.highlight-cyan} and ends with [machines that can hold the world in
their heads]{.highlight-magenta}: robots, agents, glasses that understand the room you
are standing in.

textbook]{.highlight-amber} the whole time. I will not tell you what it is yet. But you
have already seen it tonight, thousands of times.

##  {background-image="assets/content-bg.png" background-size="cover"}

[CHAPTER SEVEN · THE HERO WAS THERE ALL ALONG]{.section-label}
[The humble Gaussian [(say: GOW-see-an)]{.pronunciation}]{.slide-title}

::: {.spread}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
y = np.exp(-x**2 / 2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.1))
fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
ax.set_facecolor("none")
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from matplotlib.path import Path as MplPath
from matplotlib.patches import PathPatch
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("bell", ["#0b1026", "#46d3ff"])
grad = np.linspace(0, 1, 256).reshape(-1, 1)
im = ax.imshow(grad, extent=[-4, 4, 0, 1], origin="lower", aspect="auto",
               cmap=cmap, alpha=0.55)
clip = PathPatch(MplPath(list(zip(x, y)) + [(4, 0), (-4, 0)]),
                 transform=ax.transData, facecolor="none", edgecolor="none")
ax.add_patch(clip)
im.set_clip_path(clip)
ax.plot(x, y, color="#46d3ff", lw=2.5)
ax.axvline(0, ymax=0.93, color="#c77dff", ls="--", lw=1.5)
ax.axhline(0, color="#46d3ff", lw=2)
ax.text(0, -0.16, "mean (where)", ha="center", color="#aab4d4", fontsize=12)
ax.text(2.3, -0.16, "spread (how wide)", ha="center", color="#aab4d4", fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.12)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%" .body-text}
You have seen this curve. Exam marks. Heights. Measurement errors. The
[bell curve]{.highlight-cyan}.

It is just a soft bump: **strong in the middle, fading at the edges**. Two
numbers describe it, where its centre is and how wide it spreads.
:::

::::

::: {.quote-card}
A Gaussian is the simplest way to say: *"something is roughly here, and a
bit fuzzy around the edges."*
:::

:::

## Class reference: typography {.smaller}

`.header-label` [FUTURE SCIENCE × HKU SUMMER INSTITUTE]{.header-label}
`.header-subtext` [A muted secondary line under a header block]{.header-subtext}
`.section-label` [CYAN CHAPTER LABEL]{.section-label}
`.section-label-gold` [GOLD VARIANT FOR DARK-IMAGE SLIDES]{.section-label-gold}
`.big-title` [Display title for hero slides]{.big-title}
`.slide-title` [Content-slide title]{.slide-title}
`.subtitle` [A subtitle line under a display title]{.subtitle}
`.pronunciation` — trails a title at small size: [The humble Gaussian [(say: GOW-see-an)]{.pronunciation}]{.slide-title}

## Class reference: inline and body {.smaller}

`.big-quote` [“A standalone spoken line, large and light.”]{.big-quote}

`.body-text` with inline colour spans `.highlight-cyan` `.highlight-magenta` `.highlight-amber` `.accent`:

::: {.body-text}
Body text at reading size, with a [cyan emphasis]{.highlight-cyan}, a [magenta
emphasis]{.highlight-magenta}, an [amber emphasis]{.highlight-amber} and an [accent word]{.accent}.
:::

`.author-name` and `.author-affiliation`:

[Dr. Presenter Name]{.author-name}
[Affiliation line in the muted credit style]{.author-affiliation}

`.closing-line` centres a small final statement:

::: {.closing-line}
A closing line, centred, at footnote weight.
:::

`.narrow-text` pads the right side so prose keeps a narrow column.

Layout components (the theme's marked structural exceptions):
`.title-layout` with `.layout-top` / `.layout-middle` / `.layout-bottom` gives a
title slide its three zones (top header, centred middle, bottom credit);
`.spread` distributes a content slide's blocks evenly over the height
below the title. Both size only their own children.

## Class reference: cards {.smaller}

`.quote-card` — tinted callout with a cyan accent edge:

::: {.quote-card}
Use for definitions and asides. Border, wash and padding only: no
positioning.
:::
